clue.text: Introduction of President of Wales in year 21unlikely

indicators.note: an unlikely arrangement is an improbable one, so the letters before it are put in an order nobody would expect

blocks.note: taken as written
the source's figure here is garbled; the letters still needed are the Roman numerals for 1950, the year the clue must have named

explanation.surface: Imagining a President of Wales, an unlikely office in any year.
explanation.walkthrough: The source's '21' must stand for a year written in Roman numerals: MCML (1950) supplies exactly the C, L and two Ms that 'of Wales in year' lacks.
explanation.definitionFit: US presidents customarily open their speeches to the nation by greeting citizens with this salutation.

clue.text: Our energy generation might isolate Britain among Frenchmen

indicators.note: might hints at what the letters could become once their order is changed
among places the rearranged letters between the outer pair

blocks.note: taken as written
B is the abbreviation for Britain
MM abbreviates messieurs, French for gentlemen

explanation.surface: A political worry that a power-generation scheme might cut Britain off among the French.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Energy generation' reads as power stations, but it is the body's own chemistry.
explanation.definitionFit: Metabolism is the set of chemical processes by which living bodies produce the power they need.

clue.text: Dietary item taking a pointer from one with the scales

blocks.note: a fish is covered in scales
the forefinger is what we point with

explanation.surface: A dieter getting advice from someone holding the bathroom scales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The scales' suggests weighing; it is the scaly skin of a fish.
explanation.definitionFit: A breaded strip of white fish is a familiar food on British plates, especially for children.

clue.text: The hinge from an envelope, right?

definitions.note: loosely: the sliding support for a bureau's hinged flap

indicators.note: from says the letters are taken out of the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters span the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Checking that the flap of an envelope is what is meant by its hinge.
explanation.definitionFit: A loper is the sliding wooden bar that pulls out to support the hinged writing flap of a bureau.

clue.text: Going beyond the upright bend, a lot use gravity sadly

indicators.note: sadly suggests things have gone wrong, leaving these letters in disorder

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
g is the symbol for the acceleration due to gravity

explanation.surface: A complaint that a bend in a post has taken it past vertical, caused by gravity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The upright' reads as a post, but it is the right angle, ninety degrees.
explanation.definitionFit: A triangle with one angle greater than ninety degrees, exceeding a right angle, is described this way.

clue.text: Unfortunate few are responsible for caviare to the general

indicators.note: something unfortunate has gone awry, so the words that follow are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written, all seventeen letters

explanation.surface: A luckless minority are blamed for serving fine food to people who cannot appreciate it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caviare to the general' is Hamlet's phrase for something too refined for ordinary people; the biblical saying about casting treasures to pigs means the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Both expressions describe something valuable offered to people incapable of appreciating its worth.

clue.text: Estuarial English juvenile mimes letters and soft words

indicators.note: the London accent named here pronounces a word for youngsters in its own way, so the sound is what counts
the letters of the word are what is used, freely rearranged

blocks.note: yoof is the Estuary English way of saying youth
taken as written

explanation.surface: A teenager from the Thames estuary acting out letters and gentle words in a game of charades.
explanation.walkthrough: Estuary English is the accent of London and the Thames estuary, where youth is said 'yoof'; that sound is written EUPH.
explanation.definitionFit: A euphemism is a mild expression substituted for a harsh or blunt one.

clue.text: Halite, one of Bill Haley's crew?

blocks.note: first meaning: the mineral form of sodium chloride
second meaning: a sailor in a rock'n'roll band's crew

explanation.surface: Asking whether the mineral halite was a member of Bill Haley's band.
explanation.walkthrough: A salt is an old sailor, a member of a crew; Haley's crew played rock music.
explanation.definitionFit: Halite is the mineral name for naturally occurring crystalline sodium chloride mined underground.

clue.text: See 7
One drunk turns to the others: "Keep quiet! We are drunkards"

definitions.note: plural noun phrase, the drunks speaking of themselves

indicators.note: turning round means each word is read from its end back to its start

blocks.note: a sot is a habitual drunk
surface padding: sets the scene of the drunk addressing his companions
an order to those who are talking: stop it, as in 'stops talking'

explanation.surface: A drunk turns round to his companions, hushes them, and announces that they are all drunkards.
explanation.walkthrough: Both pieces turn: a sot becomes TOS and a hushing STOPS becomes SPOTS, giving TOSSPOTS; the S of the second piece is loosely clued.
explanation.definitionFit: Tosspot is an old word for a heavy drinker, one who tosses off pots of ale.

clue.text: A 12 point type left at the top

blocks.note: taken as written
pica is a printing type size of 12 points
L is the usual abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A typesetter's instruction to put 12-point type in the top left corner.
explanation.definitionFit: Apical describes something situated at the apex or tip, the highest point of a structure.

clue.text: Hold fire tender in esteem. O, calamity!

indicators.note: a calamity is a disaster, leaving the preceding letters wrecked and rearranged

blocks.note: to tender is to make a bid
taken as written

explanation.surface: A melodramatic cry about holding someone tender in high regard, then disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hold fire tender' reads like a soldier's command; 'tender' is a verb meaning offer.
explanation.definitionFit: To hold fire is to delay acting, waiting patiently for the right moment, which is this idiom.

clue.text: See 5
Dynasty led we British into Scott's mass of deception

blocks.note: the Tang dynasty ruled China from 618 to 907
taken as written
B is the abbreviation for British

explanation.surface: A dynasty leading the British into a deception, as in a Walter Scott novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Scott wrote in Marmion: 'Oh what a tangled web we weave, when first we practise to deceive' — note that 'led we' sits in plain sight.
explanation.definitionFit: Scott's famous line uses this image for the complicated mess of lies a deceiver creates.

clue.text: Walks over the Sedan Alps with energy

indicators.note: over as in knocked over, so the letters tumble into a new order

blocks.note: the two words taken as written, the article excluded
E is the symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Energetic hikes across the mountains near Sedan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Walks' looks like a verb but is a plural noun; Sedan is a French town, not near any Alps.
explanation.definitionFit: Esplanades are long open level paths, often along a seafront, for strolling.

clue.text: Newlyn church - hang in there!

indicators.note: the answer sits in there, inside the run of letters across the place name and the next word

blocks.note: the letters straddle the end of the Cornish town's name and the start of the building

explanation.surface: Encouragement to someone at a Cornish church to persevere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hang in there' reads as a stock phrase of encouragement, but 'hang' is the definition and 'in there' signals the concealment. Newlyn is a Cornish fishing town.
explanation.definitionFit: To lynch is to execute someone, typically by hanging, without legal trial, by mob action.

clue.text: How the Church saw Galileo here; taking it up with the State

indicators.note: in a down clue, taking a word up means reading it from bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
Cal is the abbreviation for California, a US state

explanation.surface: A history lesson on the Church's treatment of Galileo and church-state relations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The State' reads as government against Church, but it is one American state.
explanation.definitionFit: The Inquisition condemned Galileo's heliocentrism as contrary to doctrine, treating him as a heretic.

clue.text: See 1
This virago would continue to take the mickey

blocks.note: read as 'she would', contracted to she'd
to rag is to tease, and carrying on doing so is ragging on

explanation.surface: A description of a shrewish woman who never stops teasing.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one sentence about 'this virago': she'd rag on. To take the mickey is British slang for teasing.
explanation.definitionFit: A virago is a domineering, fierce woman, which is exactly what a fire-breathing female monster suggests figuratively.

clue.text: Dynast might try to hide in the chimney-back

indicators.note: to hide in something is to go inside it, so one word is tucked inside another
back, attached to the whole assembly, says to read it from the end

blocks.note: to have a go is to try
lum is a Scots and northern word for a chimney

explanation.surface: Someone powerful attempting to conceal himself at the back of a fireplace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chimney-back' looks like one hearth term but splits in two: the chimney, in its Scots form, and a signal that the whole assembly is turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: A dynast is a hereditary ruler, and the Mughal emperors of India were such a ruling line.

clue.text: One taking referrals from a saw doctor?

definitions.text: One taking referrals from a saw doctor?

blocks.clueFragment: One taking referrals from a saw doctor?
blocks.note: surface reading: a medical consultant receiving patients sent on by a GP
setter's reading: a doctor who uses a saw, on patients that are timber growing in the garden

explanation.surface: A hospital consultant receiving patients sent by a doctor with an odd name.
explanation.walkthrough: Surgeons take referrals from doctors; here the doctor's tool is a saw and the patients are oaks and elms.
explanation.definitionFit: An arborist who prunes, treats and fells timber in gardens is jokingly titled a surgeon.

clue.text: Here Wordsworth wrote lines on boy's upbringing

indicators.note: bringing a word up in a down clue reads it from bottom to top

blocks.note: RY abbreviates railway, a set of lines
a lad is a boy

explanation.surface: Wordsworth writing verse about a boy's upbringing, as in The Prelude.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lines' and 'upbringing' fit the poet's work on his own childhood, but are railway lines and a reversal. Wordsworth lived at Rydal Mount in the Lake District.
explanation.definitionFit: The poet spent his later decades living at Rydal Mount near Grasmere, writing there.

clue.text: Strike makes us work quietly in the theatre

indicators.note: in places the preceding pair inside the venue named after it

blocks.note: op is short for opus, a work
p is piano, the musical direction to play quietly
the stage stands for the theatre as a profession

explanation.surface: Industrial action means actors working softly on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'us' does no wordplay work; it belongs to the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A strike is a stoppage of work by employees as industrial protest.

clue.text: See 22
Abstraction in the medium term

blocks.note: first meaning: a dreamy, absent state of mind
second meaning: the spiritualist's word for the state in which she speaks with the dead

explanation.surface: Sounds like an economist talking about abstract planning over the medium term.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Medium term' reads as a stretch of time, but it is the term a spiritualist medium uses.
explanation.definitionFit: Abstraction means absorption or absent-mindedness, and a seance medium supposedly enters this hypnotic state to contact spirits.

clue.text: Made a dowager around noon, with pains in the ear

definitions.note: adjective: having panes, which sounds like pains

indicators.note: around says one word is wrapped about the outside of a single letter

blocks.note: a dowager is a widow holding her late husband's title
N is the abbreviation for noon

explanation.surface: A woman widowed around midday, suffering from earache.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a pun: 'pains' heard by the ear is panes of glass, so 'with pains' means having windows.
explanation.definitionFit: A building fitted with glass panes is described as having windows, a pun via sound on aches.

clue.text: Spanish cuisine bound up with the French

indicators.note: in an across clue, up still means read backwards, as if turned over

blocks.note: to bound is to leap
la is the French feminine word for the

explanation.surface: Spanish cooking closely tied up with French cooking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound up with' reads as a single phrase meaning linked to, but splits into a verb, a reversal signal and a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Paella is a Valencian rice dish with saffron, seafood and meat, a classic example of Spanish cooking.

taken as written
SJ, Society of Jesus, is the letters Jesuits put after their names
